title: AI in the Next Decade: What Can We Reasonably Predict?

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today I want to talk about prediction — specifically, the challenge of making reasonable predictions about AI's trajectory. Before I begin, I want to make an important methodological point: most predictions about technology, especially transformative technology, have historically been both underestimates and overestimates simultaneously. We tend to overestimate short-term change and underestimate long-term change.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: This is sometimes called "Amara's Law," after the American futurist Roy Amara: "We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run." Think about how many predictions of AI "revolutions" came and went in the 1980s and 1990s — followed by what became known as "AI winters." And then think about how dramatically AI has accelerated since 2017.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: So what can we say with reasonable confidence about the next ten years? First, AI will continue to improve in capability. The progress in large language models, image generation, and scientific applications over the past five years gives us strong grounds for expecting continued advancement. By 2034, AI will almost certainly be performing tasks that current systems cannot.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Second, AI will increasingly be embedded in everyday tools and processes. We won't necessarily interact with AI as a distinct entity — we already don't, in most cases. We'll be using search, writing assistance, medical diagnostics, and financial tools that have AI deeply integrated into their function. The question will not be "does this use AI?" but "how well is the AI being used here?"

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Third — and this is where it gets complicated — the social, economic, and political impacts will be deeply uneven. By 2034, some sectors will have been profoundly disrupted; others will look much as they do today. Workers in routine cognitive roles will have been significantly affected; workers in highly skilled, interpersonal, or creative roles will likely have found AI to be a useful tool rather than a threat.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Fourth, the regulatory landscape will look very different. By 2034, we will almost certainly have seen major legislation on AI across multiple jurisdictions — the EU AI Act is already in force; others will follow. Whether that regulation will be adequate, well-designed, and enforceable is a different question. Regulatory capacity has historically lagged behind technological change, and there is little reason to expect this to change rapidly.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Let me close with what I think is the most important point. The future is not a destination we are travelling to — it is something we are building, collaboratively and continuously. The AI systems that will shape life in 2034 are being trained on the data we are producing today. The regulations that will govern them are being drafted today. The educational systems that will prepare workers for that world are being designed today. Every choice matters. That is both humbling and empowering.
